note: Analyst Shark, pressed through the security angle. The plan's auth pillar (C2) has real structural gaps around the cookie mechanism it locked in D3; the journal (C3) has two integrity defects; the supervisor (C4) has blast-radius and single-instance gaps the repo's own incident history warns about.

findings.section: Phase 4 — Declarative Route Table & Default-Deny Auth; Phase 1 ANCHOR_BOOT
findings.message: The plan never states which credential authenticates MUTATING requests from the browser after the cutover, and it explicitly defers CSRF hardening as 'Butler-era'. Walk it: Phase 1 declares window.ANCHOR_BOOT the ONLY server→client state channel and says it carries 'token presence' — not the token. So post-extraction, _postJson either (a) authenticates via the D3 cookie — an AMBIENT credential the browser attaches automatically, which is exactly the precondition for CSRF against localhost:8777 and the Tailscale-exposed PWA surface (a hostile page can fire authenticated POSTs to /api/rnd/term_input2, term_kill, move_project, push_now — i.e. keystroke injection into live agent terminals and destructive project ops), or (b) reads a token exposed to page JS, which is XSS-readable and contradicts the spirit of 'no URL tokens'. Nowhere does the plan specify SameSite, HttpOnly, Secure, or cookie scope. The header-token model being replaced was CSRF-immune by construction; D3's cookie model is not, so deferring CSRF is not a scope choice — it is shipping the auth pillar with a new vulnerability class the old model lacked. Phase 4 must specify: which credential POSTs use, SameSite=Strict (or Lax + origin check in the front-door hook), HttpOnly/Secure decisions, and a CSRF test in the gate. Until then C2's 'default-deny by construction' claim is refuted: the construction has an undesigned door.

findings.section: Phase 0 cookie spike / Phase 4 cookie application
findings.message: 'Cookie set at first tokened visit' is asserted but the FIRST tokened visit is never designed. A browser navigating to / sends no token; how does John's desktop browser, and especially the iPhone/iPad PWA over Tailscale HTTPS, deliver the token the first time on each client? If the answer is a one-time ?token= URL, that contradicts the North Star's 'no URL tokens except where WS demands it' unless the plan explicitly carves out a one-shot enrollment redirect that immediately sets the cookie and strips the URL (and states the history/log exposure of that one shot). If the answer is 'type it into a login form', that is a new page and a new open route that must appear in OPEN_ROUTES. The Phase-0 spike's acceptance questions cover cookie-through-WS-upgrade but not enrollment. This is a per-client design decision (desktop, PWA, Playwright fixtures, healthcheck walk) that gates the Phase-4 ops cutover — undesigned, it surfaces as a lockout during the cutover with John's daily tool on the line (C7 adjacency).

findings.topic: single shared token across control and work planes
findings.message: Phase 5 authenticates the supervisor's IPC 'with the same ANCHOR_TOKEN secret' that Phase 4 puts in browser cookies and retains in ?token= WS URLs (which land in browser history, proxy logs, and Tailscale Serve access logs). The supervisor is the process-spawning work plane — it launches claude.exe children under John's profile. Reusing the browser-exposed credential for it means any leak of the UI credential (XSS in the freshly-extracted 4,600-line JS blob, a logged WS URL, a shared screenshot) is immediately a spawn-capable credential. D2 says 'loopback token-authed IPC'; it does not mandate the SAME token. The plan should mint a separate supervisor IPC secret (delivered via AppEnvironmentExtra to both services, never to any client/browser), or explicitly record the shared-secret blast radius as an accepted risk with John's sign-off. One line of design now; a credential-tiering retrofit later.

findings.section: Phase 3 — idempotent event-replay tool + journal-first ordering
findings.message: Journal-first ordering plus emit() fail-open guarantees a class of journal-ahead events that represent mutations that NEVER committed to the authoritative store (crash or failure between emit and the legacy write). The plan then ships an 'idempotent event-replay tool: re-applying the journal against the legacy stores converges them' as 'the operational answer to a legacy-ahead or conflict classification'. Converging the authoritative store TOWARD the journal is a partial read-path-authority inversion — the exact thing D1 and the non-goal ('NOT promoting the event log to source of truth') forbid — and it can materialize records the system never made: an orphaned job_launch_requested or session-advance intent whose legacy write failed validation gets replayed into existence. The plan calls orphaned events 'benign intent records with an idempotent replay path' — benign only if replay distinguishes intent events from state-change events and refuses to fabricate from intents. Required: replay is operator-invoked, dry-run-first (stated), restores ONLY records the journal proves existed (state-change events with completed legacy correlates elsewhere), never auto-converges, and classifies orphaned intents as a separate non-replayable census line. Otherwise the recovery tool is the mechanism by which the 'lost from an index' fix becomes a 'fabricated into an index' bug.

findings.topic: merge order violates per-writer ordering under clock regression
findings.section: The journal writer model — seq/lock semantics
findings.message: The total order is defined as a global sort by (ts, writer_id, writer_seq). Wall-clock ts is not monotonic — an NTP step-back on PUTER makes writer_seq N+1 carry an EARLIER ts than N, and the global sort then reorders a single writer's own events, violating exactly the per-writer monotonic guarantee writer_seq exists to provide. Derived views are order-sensitive (session closed vs advanced, job launched vs cancelled), so a clock step during a live run silently derives wrong state and the parity gate reports phantom BUGs — or worse, matching-but-wrong views. The fix is cheap and should be stated in the writer model: a k-way merge that preserves each segment's writer_seq order absolutely (writer_seq dominates within a writer; ts only arbitrates ACROSS writers), plus a rule for cross-writer causality (causation_id ordering wins over ts when present). As written, the deterministic merge is deterministic but not correct.

findings.topic: open GET plane persists until Phase 4 with compensating control unstated
findings.message: The known highest-severity live weakness — the unauthenticated GET data plane serving /artifact, /project, /report (including domains/commercial.md-adjacent project data) — is scheduled fifth of seven phases, behind frontend extraction and hygiene, justified only by soak stability. The implicit compensating control (127.0.0.1 bind; Tailscale exposure gated on ANCHOR_TOKEN per the anchor-as-app research) is never stated in the plan. Either state it as the accepted interim control with an explicit 'no Tailscale Serve exposure of :8777 before the Phase-4 enforce flip' invariant asserted somewhere (healthcheck or checklist), or pull a coarse whole-plane token gate into Phase 0's shim deploy. Silence leaves the risk window unowned.

This host has ALREADY had the duplicate-supervisor incident (2026-06-08: rogue Anchor-Server NSSM service racing :8777 because the old code bound with SO_REUSEADDR). The plan's install script specifies ObjectName, env cloning, and NO_WINDOW discipline — but not the IPC port assignment, the 127.0.0.1-only bind, or the SO_EXCLUSIVEADDRUSE single-instance guard the dashboard itself gained from that incident (paths.classify_bind_error/use_exclusive_bind exist and should be reused). A second service class with the same historical failure mode and none of the learned defenses is a regression waiting to recur. One sentence in Phase 5 fixes it.

findings.section: Phase 5 — IPC contract table + live probes
findings.message: Live probe (a) has the healthcheck 'ask the LIVE supervisor to spawn a trivial claude.exe --version child', implying the token-authed loopback API can be handed a command to run. If the IPC launch endpoint accepts arbitrary argv, the supervisor is an RCE-by-design endpoint gated by one shared secret (see the shared-token finding). The contract table should constrain the launch row to the guarded lane-launch path (the repo just landed 'relaunch goes through launch_guarded' — same principle), with the credentials/PATH probe as a dedicated, hardcoded probe endpoint that spawns a fixed binary, never a caller-supplied one.

findings.topic: OPEN_ROUTES candidates and token-unset semantics absent
findings.message: The plan builds the allowlist MECHANISM (checked-in table, justification strings, live-match test) but never proposes the actual candidate open set — yet deciding which routes are open IS the security decision C2 exists to force. Likewise, C2 gates the data plane 'when ANCHOR_TOKEN is set'; the plan never states what default-deny means when the token is UNSET (everything open, as today? refuse to boot? warn banner?). Both belong in the plan as Phase-4 near-term specifics: a proposed candidate list (e.g. the 401 page itself, /vendor/brand favicon, the build-mismatch 409 path) and an explicit token-unset behavior asserted by the hybrid-state healthcheck check.

findings.topic: no Host-header validation for open routes
findings.message: Whatever survives on the open allowlist remains reachable cross-origin via DNS rebinding despite the loopback bind (the browser resolves an attacker domain to 127.0.0.1 and same-origin policy no longer protects the responses; cookies won't be sent, but OPEN routes need none). A Host-header check (localhost/127.0.0.1/the Tailscale hostname) in the front-door hook is a few lines, covers every open route by construction, and closes the one attack that default-deny-with-allowlist structurally leaves open. Worth a bullet in the Phase-4 hook spec.

The ENFORCE-mode tripwire runs in the test suite; the distro-style scan covers only writes to journal/ paths. A production-only or hotfix code path that writes a legacy store WITHOUT going through a blessed wrapper is caught by neither — Tier-2 parity catches it eventually, but only for views the parity gate derives (session/effort), not for every store the census enumerated (rnd_jobs/ records, doc-persist commits). Close the triangle statically: extend the codebase-wide scan to forbid direct writes to the census-enumerated store paths from any module except the blessed wrappers, mirroring the journal.py rule. Otherwise C3's 'every mutation-of-record' claim rests on test coverage, not construction.

The warn log records who WOULD 401 and is reviewed as a gate artifact — it will therefore capture requests carrying ?token= query strings and cookie headers. State that the warn logger redacts credential values (token params, Cookie/Authorization headers) so the soak artifact isn't itself a credential store sitting in the repo or a gate attachment.

findings.topic: msvcrt.locking semantics on the cli segment
findings.section: The journal writer model — cli segment lock
findings.message: msvcrt.locking(LK_LOCK) retries for ~10 seconds then raises OSError rather than blocking indefinitely, and it locks a byte range relative to the current file position — under append the region to lock and the seek discipline need stating, and a contention-timeout needs a defined behavior (retry? fail-open into the emit-failure counter?). One sentence in the Phase-3 journal.py spec prevents an implementer from discovering these semantics mid-wave.
